newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Rangatira wins capital gains case in Privy Council.
newsitem.headline: Rangatira wins capital gains case in Privy Council.

text.p: The Privy Council have ruled that a Wellington-based company was not liable to pay tax on capital gains made in the process of buying and selling shares, the New Zealand Press Association reported on Tuesday.
The case has been seen as an important test case on capital gains.

In a reserve judgment released in London, the judicial committee of five Law Lords also ordered the respondent, the Commissioner of Inland Revenue, to pay the appellant Rangatira Ltd's costs for both the Privy Council appeal and earlier hearings in the Court of Appeal and High Court.

Rangatira, which is owned mainly by charities, had objected to a $NZ3.8 million tax bill, claiming it was not carrying on a business of buying and selling shares for profit, so it should not be taxed on capital gains.
The Inland Revenue had argued that from at least April 1983 Rangatira's share trading activity was part of its ordinary business activity and therefore taxable.
The issue at the centre of the dispute was how many transactions of buying and selling shares an investor could make before being regarded as a share trader for tax purposes.
The IRD said Rangatira had begun to make money from capital gains on share trading rather than just investing for dividend share. Rangatira had made 51 share sales over a seven-year period.

In its judgment, the Privy Council said it was not the number of the transactions during the seven-year period alone which had led the Court of Appeal to overturn the High Court's earlier decision that the capital gains were not taxable.
Rather, it was a change in company policy recorded in firm's board minutes during two meetings in 1985 and alluded to in a letter by the company's chairman, David Steele.

"Yet this conclusion was based upon Mr Steele's evidence that the ... Related transactions were exceptional, and did not reflect a change in policy of the appellant or in the nature of its business as a whole," the Law Lords said.

"The Solicitor-General (John McGrath) suggested that the Court of Appeal would have been entitled to discount to some extent the weight which should be placed on Mr Steele's evidence, because it could hardly be regarded as impartial.
"Their Lordships do not accept this suggestion.

"Looking at the matter in retrospect their Lordships would think that the decision could have gone either way, but that is not to say that it was wrong...The decision of (the High Court) Justice Gallen was one which he was entitled to reach, and one which should not have been reversed."

The Privy Council's decision could have further tax implications for other investment funds. Earlier reports suggest that the ruling will help remove uncertainty over the taxation of capital gains when buying and selling shares.
